Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
People who are related to the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: make sure to stay close to exit
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

issues.item: Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
issues.explanation: The loss-themed trigger is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. It implies bereavement-related activation, but there are no corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal items about death, losing a loved one, or grief. In this profile it stands out as clinically mismatched rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: Avoiding authority figures or uniforms is not well linked to the reported trauma type or the rest of the profile. For intimate-partner physical abuse, this strategy would need supporting material suggesting the perpetrator was an authority figure or that uniforms became trauma cues, but no such trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items are present. It therefore looks disconnected from the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
At 63, Matiu had spent most of his adult life working construction, and he still measured himself by whether he could keep moving, keep lifting, keep handling what came his way. The abuse began in the years before his wife died, in a later relationship that people around him assumed was simply “difficult.” In private, his partner would grab him hard by the jaw and neck during arguments, sometimes digging her fingers into his arm or shoving him backward when she felt ignored. What stayed with him was not only the pain but the humiliation of standing in his own house, seeing her hands come toward his face and throat, and feeling himself freeze rather than stop her. Men he knew did not talk about being physically overpowered by a partner, and Matiu had come away from those moments certain that something fundamental in him had failed.

In the months after the relationship ended, reminders of the abuse began catching him off guard in ways that felt immediate and bodily. Seeing certain body parts could set him off, especially hands closing around someone’s wrist, a thumb pressed under a chin, or a forearm lifted too quickly in conversation. Even on a work site, if one of the younger guys clapped another man on the shoulder or two workers started arguing face-to-face, Matiu felt his body tense before he had fully registered what he had seen. If someone asked directly about that relationship, or if he heard the story retold by people connected to it, he felt exposed and ashamed, as if the scene were happening again and proving the same thing about him. In those moments he was flooded by the thought that he was weak and that he could not rely on himself even to protect his own body.

Because of that, he began shaping his days around getting out quickly and keeping himself soothed. At job briefings he stood near the edge of the group and picked the spot closest to an exit without seeming obvious about it. If there was any chance of disagreement with a foreman or coworker, he backed off early, telling himself it was better not to let anything escalate. When the memories were stirred up after seeing one of those physical reminders, or after a cousin mentioned his former partner’s name, he would stop at hardware stores or discount shops after work and buy things he did not need—tools, jackets, kitchen gadgets—just to blunt the churn in his chest for an hour or two. The spending gave him a brief sense of relief, but it was relief by distraction rather than comfort.

His body had also become organized around danger. He startled violently at ordinary sounds on site—metal dropping, a nail gun firing unexpectedly, a truck gate slamming—and once his heart was racing he became even more alert to the kinds of visual details that hooked him, noticing hands, arms, shoulders, who was standing close to whom. Entering any building, from the site trailer to a diner, he scanned immediately for exits. At night he woke and checked the apartment, looking to see whether he was safe, listening at the door, orienting himself before he could settle again. That constant readiness fed directly into the ways he tried to manage himself: sitting where he could leave fastest, keeping out of arguments, arranging his life so he would never be trapped.

Over time, those habits began to change what he believed about himself. Each time he moved to the door before a union meeting had even started, or swallowed a complaint rather than risk confrontation, it confirmed his private conviction that he was not a man who could stand his ground. The impulsive purchases embarrassed him afterward when he saw the unopened bags in his apartment, and the embarrassment settled into a familiar judgment: he was weak, he had no real control, he could not rely on himself. He described feeling dead inside much of the time, especially on weekends, sitting among things he had bought and not wanted, unable to feel much except tiredness and self-disgust.

The cycle tightened because the strategies that were meant to protect him kept his world organized around the abuse. Staying near exits meant he was always noticing who blocked a doorway or whose body was between him and the room’s edge. Avoiding conflict made him acutely watchful for the first sign that a conversation might turn tense. Refusing to talk about what had happened made any direct mention of it land with even more force when it slipped through. On the construction site this had become costly: he kept to himself, passed up chances to correct mistakes, and once left a planning meeting early after two men started arguing across the table, later telling his supervisor he felt sick.

What finally brought Matiu in was a night when he woke abruptly, checked the locks three times, and then sat in the dark feeling nothing except certainty that this was what the rest of his life would be. The next day at work, a coworker reached out suddenly to get his attention and Matiu flinched so hard he nearly dropped a tool. He was frightened by how small his life had become—organized around doors, noise, and not provoking anyone—and by how fully he believed the abuse had revealed his true character. What he wanted, though he said it cautiously, was to stop living as if every room might turn on him, and to find out whether feeling dead inside had to be permanent.
